Neither threats nor insults deprive the enemy of strength. That is what matters: depriving him of strength. That is also the standard by which one should receive such insults.
Do they take strength away from me?
Only to the extent that I spend time on them and think about them.

Theodor Haecker said in 1917 that the old medieval cathedrals must cry out for their own destruction when the aesthetic literary class covers them in the slobbering cultural and educational slime of this kind.
If that is true, then our old German cities were rightly destroyed. But does the same not apply to every one of us who feels spat upon by that cultural slime?
Should I not also cry out for this cultural brothel finally to be destroyed?
We are taken at our word. This is the age of existentialism.
Spirit finds executors and people willing to carry things through who are themselves without spirit and who perform the work of the knacker’s yard and the levelling ground.
Yet as accelerators against their own will, they end up accelerating things entirely different from those they themselves wanted to accelerate.

To a legal scholar: I have reread the good old Hall, International Law, in Higgins’s edition (8th ed., Oxford, 1924). He is old, and probably old-fashioned too, but that is exactly what makes him so instructive and so superior to positivists of the Strupp, Lauterpacht, etc. variety. His criticism of the doctrine that an occupying power exercises the sovereignty of the occupied country deserves very close attention: this would “enable to brand acts of resistance on the part of an invaded population with a stigma of criminality which is as useless as it is unjust.” Hall even has a separate chapter entitled “Postliminium.” The whole thing, in this 1924 edition, is a good example of how English jurists never experienced the break with the pre-positivist tradition that had such catastrophic consequences in Germany. I already noticed this years ago when reading Westlake.

Then there is the question of how to distinguish the theatre of war from occupied territory, especially the meaning of autorité établie—“established authority”; the difference between the executive authority of the military commander in the two cases; and the question whether, in occupied territory, this executive authority of the military commander is not itself shaped, in its organization and internal structure, by the constitutional structure of the occupying state. Here too the Hague Regulations remain at the standard of 1907, including in the relationship between military and civilian authority.

(I am deeply grateful to you simply for the possibility of talking about these things with you and telling you what is on my mind.) I am often tormented by what I call the “impatience of justice,” and it is an immense comfort to know that you understand the intention and intellectual impulse behind my way of practising legal scholarship. It matters not in the least whether, in the end, you agree or disagree with my conclusions. Your visit to Plettenberg continues to bear fruit even now, and nothing could give me greater pleasure than the further certainty that there is complete reciprocity between us in this respect. Then 21 April 1948 and 1 May 1948: Formosus, Titulus, Sallust.

Belgium, which you have come to know, has become a peculiar centre from which the destruction of the classical law of war first began. Neutrality was originally devised to guarantee security, and <…> the atomic bomb stripped that security away. You will read something in the Nomos about the genuine and great scholar Ernest Nys. But also read note 39 in my The Concept of the Discriminating War; and remember Cardinal Mercier’s Christmas pastoral letter of 1914: the legitimate authority is and remains the government of the occupied state, not the occupying power. In itself that is correct. Here, however, it was meant in a discriminatory sense and had a discriminatory effect, with the result that even the remarkable, classically developed institution of occupatio bellica—military occupation—was destroyed by it.

I came across the sentence L’initié tue l’initiateur—the initiate kills the initiator—and thought of W. Fraenger’s Grand Master of the Free Brotherhood, who was overcome by his pupil Hieronymus Bosch.
There is a mysterious cruelty in this world of initiation and mystery. The état d’esprit, the state of mind, is even crueller than Hobbes’s état de nature, the state of nature.

Here the son kills the father, the young kills the old; Zeus kills Cronus, Cronus kills Uranus. This eternal and biologically obvious process is reflected in the mysteries. They reveal, precisely by concealing it, the core of things.

Against this, Christianity, as a religion of the Father, is the true religion of peace: remaining in the Father’s house; the return of the prodigal son; the Ascension of Christ; Christ himself is the prodigal son. But there is no suggestion that the prodigal son brought some of the companions from his dissolute life back home with him. So how is the noble prodigal son supposed to take one of us back to the Father?

Let us therefore return to nature! But that means nothing other than this: let us kill our fathers, our teachers, our initiators, our creators, our benefactors. And at the same time: let us make sure that we ourselves never become fathers, teachers, initiators, creators, or benefactors!
The programme of Bakunin’s anarchism combined with Western individualism.
A prediction for a consistently Americanized world.
The true German—that is, the productive German—is still more likely to be a Bakuninist than an Americanist.
Do not let yourselves be deceived about that.

Homo homini homo: man is man to man. That means nothing more than standing still, marking time at the zero point of a purely polar concept, which immediately splits in opposite directions: left and right, down and up; homo homini lupus or deus—man is either a wolf or a god to man.

The typical neutralization at this dead centre consists in refusing to let the split happen, or at least postponing it. One would rather stand still: on the knife-edge, right on the boundary, balanced to the finest possible degree in the transcendental space between the transcendent and the empirical; committed to nothing, keeping every option open, remaining in the undisturbed purity of the concept. But this is an untouched purity, which means an unrealized purity. It belongs to German idealism, from pure reason all the way to pure unreason.
How, then, did the fall into hell, into utter impurity, happen?
We lived through it and came to understand it.
What has happened in Germany since 1918?

Out of the darkness of social, moral, and intellectual nothingness, out of the pure lumpenproletariat, out of the refuge of homeless non-culture, rose the unknown soldier of the First World War: until then a completely empty individual, who now filled himself with the words and passions of educated Germany at that time.
H. S. Chamberlain introduced and initiated him at Wahnfried. With that, he was admitted into the temple of culture. And he took it seriously—with the seriousness of an animal.
The passions and formulas that were offered to him.

Concepts such as deed, will, power, race, genius, Führer, charisma. And conversely, these passions and formulas, which until then had been thought in a fairly pure and abstract way, were surprised and delighted that someone was finally taking them seriously.
Now there was a man who took them seriously, who made them serious: nothing but a realizer, someone to whom one could leave the rest, nothing but an executor and enforcer.
Through sheer “carrying-through,” the I comes into being—Fichte.
The pure executor of ideas that had until then remained so pure.
This individual read enormously, in order to fuel himself.
From Mirko Jelusich’s historical novels he learned how the great men of world history talk—“these brainless fools,” Julius Caesar is fond of saying in Jelusich—and how they destroy peoples.
So here is the intellectual-historical formula for those twelve years: the great historical opera of the pure execution—that is, nothing but execution—of the pure German cult of genius.
A man condemned by history to act: Schiller’s great theme, and the great theme of his concept of tragedy.
Three ugly jabs, poisonous and yellowish, delivered in that spiteful voice:
The mention of Freisler. Curiously, Carl Brinkmann and Helmut Rumpf do the same thing. Ecco: where is the common source here?
A sentence such as: “The hatred directed at me is found only among people who do not know me, whereas the hatred directed at you exists precisely among people who do know you.”
The matter of “Stahl” must have harmed you greatly.
Yes indeed, you money-minded idealist. It harmed me greatly. Curious, once again, how well informed you are.

Gottfried Benn is magnificent in The Ptolemaic Man: One must be honest whatever the danger. But, by the way, what dangers do these continents really have to offer? Bourgeois dangers. Death is too far outside the human world to be degraded into a mere “danger.”
“I turn a disc and am myself turned; I am a Ptolemaic man.”
I do not groan like Jeremiah, nor like Paul. I do what appears before me. I am not “thrown,” and I do not drape myself in wife, child, and summer cottage either.
Existentially understood, that is the death blow to utopia.
The existentialists: the new Captains of Köpenick.

For the isolated individual struggling to maintain himself, and especially for the great “untimely” individuals—those who are precisely suited to the wrong time—the objective powers automatically become relative.
One must therefore always ask what each of these objective forces—the state, the Church—means at that particular moment in relation to the isolated person.
When Bruno Bauer speaks of the Catholic Church, for example, he constantly means different things depending on its relationship to himself.

Around 1870 he values the Catholic Church not only as a counterweight to the coming ruler of the world. It has also become something different for him from what it was in 1843, when he still regarded it as Judaism in its purest form.
The same applies to the Prussian state, to Judaism, and so on.
What else is an isolated individual supposed to do? He jumps from one sheet of ice to another.

For Barbey d’Aurevilly, the great teacher of Léon Bloy, the Catholic Church was—not only, but also—the high balcony from which he could spit down onto the heads of the rabble of his age. And then there is Nietzsche, with his use and exploitation of every value, his thousand escapes and hiding places. That is existentialism in its pure form.
The moment it is taught from university chairs, of course, it becomes comic.

Then comes a cramped, convulsive moment of mutual revenge: the empty individual takes revenge on the objective powers and uses them merely as instruments of power for his own empty ego; and the objective powers take revenge for this abuse on an individual who has become crazed by his own ego.
An idea takes possession of an individual and, by doing so, always appears in the world as a foreign guest.
The foreign guest was Adolf. He was foreign almost to the point of caricature.
Foreign precisely because of the antiseptic, empty purity of his ideas about the Führer, charisma, genius, and race. He was an executor with no prior commitments or assumptions.
The mass of educated people was uneducated.
The few genuinely educated people were still standing with Goethe and Carus. They had not yet experienced the crisis of 1848.
Bruno Bauer and Max Stirner were regarded as comic oddballs.
Adolf, by contrast, who intellectually was less than Max, was regarded even by educated men such as Popitz as a genius.
And so he entered into appearance.
“Existentialism” is the appropriate word: it therefore also delivers the death blow to this cult of genius inherited from eighteenth- and nineteenth-century Germany.

This key concept in intellectual history—the genius as executor—also clarifies my personal relationships with Franz Kluxen, who initiated me into the thoroughly genius-centred intellectual world of nineteenth-century Germany, into Richard Wagner and Otto Weininger, and with Hugo Ball, who suffered under the German cult of genius without ever overcoming it.
Ball fled from his age into humility, after having first fallen deeply into that age.
Existentialism kills the cult of genius?
The decisive step around 1900 was the transition from the Goethean cult of genius to the Hölderlinian one. That is where Heidegger remained.
What a betrayal of Kierkegaard, of Bruno Bauer, and of the Christianity that was discovered—and rediscovered—in about 1840.
“Youth without Goethe” (Max Kommerell): for us, from about 1910 onward, that meant in concrete terms youth with Hölderlin.

It meant the transition from an optimistic, peace-seeking, neutralizing cult of genius to a pessimistic, activist, tragic cult of genius. But it remained within the cult of genius and, in fact, deepened it to infinite depths.
Norbert von Hellingrath is more important than Stefan George and Rilke.
Not only the idea, but power too, appears only as a foreign guest.

When analysed as a historical fact, power is always also powerlessness, compulsion, prison. The earthly ruler who seems all-powerful becomes completely cut off from everyone else and therefore completely powerless. This is the dialectic of absolutism and sovereignty.
In the end, the absolute sovereign sits in the icy loneliness of his omnipotence, blocked off by antechambers and chiefs of staff. That is power as it appears in the world.
Probably only by saying that idea, being, and power are one and the same.
The source of all the errors and dehumanizations lies in the fact that this unity was misunderstood in empirical, positivist terms. This also gives me the connection with the note of 27 April 1948.
